prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "H World Group Ltd" (ticker HTHT), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "HTHT", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: H World Group Limited
result.industry: Hotel operator and franchisor (mainly limited-service hotels in China)
markets: China economy hotels (HanTing, Hanting Inn, Ibis)
China midscale and upper-midscale hotels (JI, Orange, Crystal Orange, Mercure, Manxin, Starway)
Upscale and lifestyle hotels in China (Blossom House, Joya, Steigenberger)
Europe and Southeast Asia hotels via H World International (Steigenberger, IntercityHotel, MAXX, Jaz, Zleep)
Hotel franchising and management services for owners

mission.plain: H World says it wants to grow as a brand-led, high-quality hotel group for China's mass market and become a world-class Chinese hotel company.

about.plain: H World runs China's biggest family of everyday hotel brands, like HanTing, JI and Orange. Most hotels are owned by other people who pay H World a fee to use its name, booking app and way of running hotels. It also owns or rents a few hundred hotels itself, plus German Steigenberger and IntercityHotel hotels in Europe. At mid-2026 it had 13,539 hotels with about 1.34 million rooms.
about.customers: Business travellers, tourists and families in China who want a clean, reliable room at a fair price, plus hotel owners who franchise its brands.
about.everyday: If you have stayed at a HanTing or JI Hotel in a Chinese city, you have used H World.

money.plain: room nights and food at its own hotels in China and Europe
fees from owners who use its brands and systems
membership, supply-chain and tech services to hotels
JI and other brands in Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia (6 hotels at Q1 2026)

result.summary: H World has a real advantage built on scale: 13,539 hotels, a 245-million-room-night H Rewards loyalty base and a central booking and tech system that franchisees pay to join. Its moat is strongest in China's mid-priced chain segment, but rivals like Jin Jiang, Atour and BTG are also large and same-hotel RevPAR has been falling, so pricing power is limited.

pricingPower.evidence: China blended ADR rose 2.6% to RMB298 in Q2 2026 but occupancy fell 1.2 points and same-hotel RevPAR fell 3.0%, and Q4 2025 same-hotel RevPAR fell 2.5%; fee income grows mainly from adding hotels (M&F revenue +23.1% in 2025), not from raising room rates.

moats.evidence: HanTing, JI and Orange are widely known in China and H Rewards members booked 245 million room nights in 2025 (+21.5%), but the brands are value brands with little premium outside China.
Franchised owners sign multi-year contracts and rely on H World's booking, revenue-management and procurement systems, but owners can and do rebrand at contract end (157 M&F closures in Q2 2026).
More hotels in 1,461 Chinese cities make the H Rewards program and app more useful to travellers, which sends more direct bookings to owners and attracts more franchisees.
With 1.26 million rooms at end-2025 (No. 4 worldwide in the HOTELS 2026 ranking), H World spreads technology, marketing and procurement over a huge base, earning a 26.9% operating margin in 2025.
China's hotel market is large and fragmented and new chains such as Atour keep entering, so there is no natural limit on rivals.
Its franchise model is the same one used by Jin Jiang, BTG, Marriott and Hilton, so rivals face no conflict in copying it.
Twenty years of standardized operations, a self-built hotel tech stack and brand upgrades such as JI Hotel 5.0 let it open 2,400+ hotels in 2025 while keeping quality consistent.
It holds master-franchise rights for Accor's Mercure, Ibis and Ibis Styles in China, but has no exclusive asset that rivals cannot get.

customers.evidence: H Rewards member room nights rose 21.5% to 245 million in 2025 and 10.7% to 60 million in Q1 2026, showing heavy repeat use; China occupancy stayed near 80% (79.8% in Q2 2026).

talent.evidence: Management is long-tenured (CEO Jin Hui was the company's first employee in 2005), but H World does not appear on major global employer rankings and hotel frontline pay is modest.

product.evidence: Its JI and Orange brands are leaders in China's midscale segment and the group is the 4th largest hotel company in the world by rooms, but rival Atour is often seen as having the more premium upper-midscale product.

competitors.name: Jin Jiang International (Jin Jiang Hotels)
competitors.note: Largest Chinese hotel group by rooms (1.55 million in 2025) with 7 Days, Vienna, Lavande and Louvre Hotels; competes brand-by-brand in economy and midscale.

competitors.name: BTG Hotels (Homeinns)
competitors.note: Home Inn, Yitel and Jianguo brands; 554,919 rooms in 2025, a direct economy and midscale rival.

competitors.name: Atour Lifestyle Holdings
competitors.note: Fast-growing upper-midscale chain (2,015 hotels at end-2025) competing with JI, Orange and Crystal Orange.

competitors.name: GreenTree Hospitality Group
competitors.note: Economy and midscale franchised hotels in lower-tier Chinese cities.

competitors.name: Dossen International Group
competitors.note: Private Chinese mid-priced chain (Dossen, Yunik) with about 227,000 rooms.

competitors.name: Delonix Group
competitors.note: Large private Chinese hotel group (about 250,000 rooms, estimated, in the HOTELS 2026 ranking) competing in economy and midscale.

competitors.name: Marriott International
competitors.note: Competes in China upper-midscale and upscale (Fairfield, Four Points, Courtyard) and in Europe.

competitors.name: Hilton Worldwide
competitors.note: Hampton by Hilton and Hilton Garden Inn compete with JI and Orange in China upper-midscale; also in Europe.

competitors.name: InterContinental Hotels Group
competitors.note: Holiday Inn Express is one of the largest foreign midscale brands in China.

competitors.name: Accor
competitors.note: Partner (H World master-franchises Ibis and Mercure in China) and competitor in Europe against Steigenberger and IntercityHotel.

competitors.name: Wyndham Hotels & Resorts
competitors.note: Franchised Ramada and Wyndham hotels in China's midscale segment.

competitors.name: Hyatt Hotels
competitors.note: Hyatt Place and lifestyle brands in China's upscale segment.

competitors.name: Trip.com Group
competitors.note: Main online travel agency; a key distribution partner that also competes for the direct customer relationship.

competitors.name: Meituan
competitors.note: Large hotel booking platform for lower-priced rooms and independent hotels.

estimates.name: Jin Jiang Hotels (estimate; not an SEC filer)
BTG Hotels (estimate; not an SEC filer)

marketShare.market: Hotel rooms of the world's 10 largest hotel groups (HOTELS magazine 2026 ranking; share of the top-10 total)

threats: Falling same-hotel RevPAR in China (-3.0% in Q2 2026, -2.5% in Q4 2025) as hotel supply grows faster than travel demand
Strong rivals in the mid-priced segment (Atour, Jin Jiang's Vienna, BTG) competing for the same franchisees
Online platforms (Trip.com, Meituan, Douyin) taking a larger share of bookings and commissions
Weak Chinese consumer spending and business-travel budgets
Franchisee economics: if owners' returns fall, signings slow and closures rise
H World International losses or weakness from Middle East conflict and Southeast Asia expansion (HWI revenue -5.8% in Q2 2026)
China-US tensions and possible delisting or audit rules affecting a Chinese ADR

ceo.name: Jin Hui (Hui Jin)
ceo.background: Company's first employee (joined 2005), former president; BSc psychology from East China Normal University, executive master's from CEIBS

c1.evidence: H World is a leader in China's chain-hotel industry, which is still consolidating (it opened 2,400+ hotels in 2025), but hotels are a mature industry rather than an emerging one.

c2.evidence: Owners choose it for its 245-million-room-night H Rewards demand engine and tech systems, and guests for consistent value at HanTing and JI, but rivals like Jin Jiang and Atour offer similar packages.

c3.evidence: HanTing and JI are household names among Chinese travellers, but H World is not the default global leader and Jin Jiang is larger by rooms (1.55 million vs 1.26 million in 2025).

c4.evidence: Its public messaging focuses on 'brand-led, high-quality growth' and the asset-light model rather than an inspiring purpose-driven mission.

c6.evidence: “affordable, clean, everywhere” is the common impression of HanTing and JI hotels in China; it is mostly positive but little known outside China and seen as mass-market.

c7.evidence: China's hotel chain share is still rising and hotel GMV grew 16.4% to RMB108.1 billion in 2025, but the underlying travel market grows slowly and RevPAR is under pressure.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into Southeast Asia (Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia) and upscale brands, and owns Steigenberger in Europe, but these are small (122 HWI hotels at June 2026).

m1.evidence: CEO Jin Hui has a clear plan for asset-light, brand-led growth and AI-driven operations, though the bigger vision is often credited to founder-chairman Ji Qi.

m2.evidence: Jin Hui is not the founder but has worked at the company since its start in 2005 and acts as a long-term insider, while founder Ji Qi remains chairman.

m4.evidence: There is little public evidence about Jin Hui's leadership style toward employees and customers.

m5.evidence: The company has built a strong in-house tech and product culture (self-built hotel systems, JI Hotel 5.0, Hanting Inn launched 2026), largely shaped by founder Ji Qi.

m6.evidence: Jin Hui rose through hotel development and operations and is hands-on with the product, but has a psychology rather than an engineering background.

m7.evidence: There is no notable public record of Jin Hui's character or causes beyond running the business.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech at a top university by Jin Hui was found.

m8b.evidence: Jin Hui keeps a low public profile; founder Ji Qi is the better-known personality.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in October 2021, revenue rose from RMB12.8 billion (2021) to RMB25.3 billion (2025) and the network grew from 7,830 to 12,858 hotels.

m10.evidence: The shift to franchising kept capital spending low (RMB838 million in 2025 vs RMB1,776 million in 2020), but the company is not specifically known for frugality.

c10.evidence: It gives hundreds of millions of Chinese trips an affordable, standard room (245 million member room nights in 2025), but its impact is mostly limited to China.

p2.evidence: Running 13,000+ hotels to a consistent standard is operationally hard, but hotels are not technologically hard or critical to the world.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year from 2020 to 2025: RMB10.2bn, 12.8bn, 13.9bn, 21.9bn, 23.9bn and 25.3bn.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from -16.5% in 2020 and 1.3% in 2021 to 26.9% in 2025, and revenue less hotel operating costs reached 39.4% of revenue in 2025.

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 cash and short-term investments of RMB15.6 billion exceeded bank debt of RMB4.2 billion and equity was RMB14.2 billion positive, though lease liabilities add about RMB30 billion.

f4.evidence: Operating income went from a RMB1.7bn loss in 2020 to RMB6.8bn in 2025 and operating cash flow from RMB0.6bn to RMB8.4bn (with a small dip in 2024 to RMB7.5bn).

v1.evidence: For a traveller in China, JI or HanTing offers a reliable, well-located, fairly priced room in almost any city, but Atour or Vienna can be equally good choices.

v2.evidence: H World does not appear in major global employer rankings such as Fortune's or Glassdoor's best places to work.

c5.evidence: Millions of Chinese business travellers and thousands of franchise owners would miss its network and booking system, though other chains could fill most of the gap.
